name: Düsseldorf and Kling Klang
hook: A self-built studio in a former factory space, where a band decided rock music should sound nothing like rock music.
blurb: Ralf Hütter and Florian Schneider set up Kling Klang, their own studio in Düsseldorf, in 1970, and from 1975 it was Kraftwerk's own label too. There they built custom instruments and wrote music that rejected American and British rock entirely, at their own pace and outside any record company's schedule, which is part of why their catalogue is so small and so tightly controlled. The scene around it was less about nightlife than about studio work: a deliberate search for a German electronic sound after a war that had made "German culture" a loaded phrase, avoiding the American blues-rock language most of their contemporaries still used.
geopolitics: West Germany's postwar generation, coming of age in the late 1960s, was reckoning openly with the Nazi period for the first time, and much of the era's German rock and experimental music (labeled 'krautrock' by the British press) was an explicit attempt to build a new cultural identity that owed nothing to either American pop culture or Germany's own recent past.
whatWasNew: Electronic music built entirely from synthesizers, drum machines, and vocoders, performed with a deliberately flat, mechanical stage presence, at a time when 'electronic' still mostly meant an experimental sideline to a rock band's real instruments.
production: Kling Klang studio, built and continually modified by the band themselves, including custom-built electronic percussion and voice synthesis equipment not commercially available elsewhere.
labels: Released through Philips and later EMI in Europe, while retaining ownership of the Kling Klang studio and, from 1975, their own vanity label for the master recordings.
politics: Rarely explicit in lyrics, but the concept itself, mechanized, depersonalized, and proudly German, was a political statement about what postwar German art could be.
